claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating has an FCC matrix.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has high elastic modulus and stable wear resistance at 300 K.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has low stacking-fault energy.
Low stacking-fault energy promotes planar slip and dislocation pile-ups in the coating.
In CoCrFeMnNi, stacking-fault energy increases with increasing temperature.
Increasing stacking-fault energy suppresses stacking-fault and nanotwin formation in CoCrFeMnNi.
At low temperature, low stacking-fault energy stabilizes extended dislocations and stacking faults.
Stabilized stacking faults create barriers to dislocation motion that enhance wear resistance.
High stacking-fault energy forces dislocations to cross-slip.
Cross-slip leads to rapid dislocation multiplication, dynamic recovery, and a disordered state.
Thermally induced lattice disorder causes lattice softening and a sharp decline in wear resistance.
Thermal activation overcomes the energy barrier for stacking-fault formation and thereby collapses dislocation-mediated plasticity into rapid lattice disorder.
A sharp decline in wear resistance and elastic modulus occurs at a critical temperature.
The critical transition changes deformation from planar slip to cross-slip-dominated deformation and rapid lattice disorder.
At 300 K, the coating has high dislocation density but controlled slip.
The critical temperature is the temperature at which stacking-fault energy becomes positive and high enough to suppress planar slip, or at which thermal energy induces rapid atomic disorder.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to FCC high-entropy alloys with low initial stacking-fault energy.
The mechanism may not apply to BCC refractory high-entropy alloys because they use different deformation mechanisms.
No exact critical temperature can be specified for FeNiCrCoCu because the cited evidence contains no system-specific stacking-fault-energy versus temperature data.
The mechanism is extrapolated from CoCrFeMnNi and general high-entropy-alloy behavior rather than demonstrated for FeNiCrCoCu.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says thermal activation overcomes a barrier for stacking-fault formation, implying enhanced fault formation, whereas the mechanism says temperature raises stacking-fault energy and suppresses stacking-fault formation.

The critical temperature is given two non-equivalent definitions—an SFE threshold that suppresses planar slip or the onset of rapid atomic disorder—without establishing that they occur at the same temperature.
